title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #298 | DOCTOR TURNED AGENT HUSTLING FOR A KL PROPERTY
excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.

qa.asker: Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: Mr J is 27 and lives in Melaka. He resigned as a government doctor to study a one-year master's in health tech, finishing in late 2026, and earns occasional income as a part-time property agent. Counting money market funds, cash, stocks and an insurance savings plan, he has about RM380,000, and he spends about RM2,000 a month. He is a client of a property investment club, can borrow RM600,000 to RM700,000, and wants a unit of about RM400,000 for cash flow, though he doesn't know KL or Selangor.
qa.question: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?
qa.quote: Don't buy any properties before 6 months income from your new job.
qa.answer: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.

reasons.title: Invest where people move for work
reasons.body: Sean always recommends main city centres such as KL, JB, Penang and Kuching, because fresh graduates head to the capital for jobs and rooms there are in short supply: about RM700 for a small room and RM1,200 for a master bedroom around Cheras. JB prices near the RTS link have already run up.

reasons.title: View matters only at the extremes
reasons.body: A KLCC or KL skyline view earns a premium for luxury and short-stay units, and a unit facing another tower 30 m away loses out. For a unit bought on rent versus instalment, view hardly matters, but floor level does in dense areas like Mont Kiara or Bangsar South, where low floors sit in the shadow of the next tower.

reasons.title: Completed units let you roll faster
reasons.body: A new launch can take four years before it earns rent you can show the bank. A completed or nearly completed unit can be let within months, and six months of declared rent helps you qualify for the next loan; developers also negotiate harder near completion.

reasons.title: His cash is well placed
reasons.body: Money market funds and savings keep him liquid while he has no steady income. With RM2,000 a month in spending, RM110,000 in the bank covers about four years, more than he needs as a buffer.

actions: Watch videos of KL and Selangor areas, then visit them: ride the LRT, walk the malls and get a feel for each address.
Join site tours if your investment club runs them, and view about 20 properties within your budget.
Stay within the RM400,000 range you are comfortable with, below the most you can borrow.
Plan who will manage the unit for you if you buy far from where you live.
Leave room in your savings for a wedding if marriage is likely in the next few years.
qa.caveat: Property investment beyond two or three units suits people who enjoy driving around, viewing buildings and dealing with strangers; if that drains you, stopping after using your two 90% loans is enough. Sean's thoughts on stocks in the episode are, in his words, not financial advice.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #298. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2025. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the club Mr J belongs to, not its owner.
